title: The Battle of Hastings
description: October 1066. William of Normandy's invasion army faces King Harold's Anglo-Saxon shield wall on Senlac Hill. The player commands the Norman force and must break the shield wall through feigned retreats and combined cavalry-archer assaults before nightfall ends the battle.

issues_found: 2,400 oak trees on a 120x120 map turns Senlac Hill into dense forest; the battle was fought on an open ridge with the Andredsweald only at the Saxon rear, and heavy woodland also makes cavalry charges and feigned retreats physically implausible.
Scattered economic furniture (10 gold mines, 8 stone mines, 16 forage bushes, 12 sheep, 8 deer) belongs to a settlement map, not a single-day set-piece battle.

Both armies are given Town Centers and Houses (and the Anglo-Saxons a Monastery, Archery Range/Barracks/Stable for the Normans); neither side had a town or ecclesiastical base on the battlefield — Harold's army had marched from Stamford Bridge and William's was camped at Hastings.

The 'Fyrd Lured' turning point fires only DISPLAY_INSTRUCTIONS twice — the feigned retreat and the resulting break in the shield wall are narrated but never mechanically modelled (no unit tasking, ownership change, or AI reaction), so the battle's decisive tactic is text only.
Only 2 archers on the Anglo-Saxon side and no Norman crossbows/heavy infantry mass; the Norman force of 30 combatants is thin for depicting three lines (archers, infantry, cavalry).
Closing narration that William's claim 'stands unopposed' overstates the outcome — resistance continued through 1066-71.

2400 oak trees blanket a 120x120 map; Senlac Hill was fought over open slope and cultivated ground, with the Andredsweald woods only to the English rear — the forest density misrepresents the battlefield
Both sides are given Town Centers, Houses, a Monastery, an Archery Range, Barracks and Stable; Hastings was a single-day encounter battle with no settlement, fortification or production on the field
Gold mines, stone mines, forage bushes, sheep and deer are placed as economic resources, which has no correspondence to a one-day pitched battle and invites base-building play
No explicit terrain elevation is evident in the placed content for 'Senlac Hill', the defining tactical feature of the battle (the English held the high ground)
Norman force lacks any infantry beyond 6 spearmen; William's centre contained a substantial dismounted infantry contingent alongside the cavalry and archers
Anglo-Saxon Monastery is an odd inclusion for an army encamped overnight on a ridge
Closing text ('Duke William's claim to the English throne stands unopposed') overstates the outcome — resistance continued through 1066–71 (Exeter, the North, Ely)
